claim: A market-neutral long-short portfolio whose signal (sent_accel) is built from LLM-extracted structured features (polarity, magnitude, event_type, tense, specificity, novelty) from EDGAR 8-K filings and GDELT 2.0 financial news, using the formula: raw_pol = polarity*magnitude per article; short_ma = 5-day rolling mean; long_ma = 20-day rolling mean; accel = short_ma - long_ma; score = -1*(cs_rank(accel)-0.5); smoothed = 30-day moving average (Alpha101 decay); rank-weighted dollar-neutral portfolio, GICS sector-neutralized, 5-day holding, weekly rebalance. On a point-in-time S&P 100 universe, Q1 2022-Q4 2024 OOS (753 trading days), net of 5bps round-trip cost: Sharpe +0.784, max drawdown 3.33%, beta_mkt +0.001, alpha +0.72bps/day with t-stat +1.345 (below 1.96 significance), 9/12 positive quarters. The frozen hyperparameter configuration failed its own pre-registered H2-2021 validation gate (IR=-1.50) and was carried forward via an author-documented override.
quote: long firms whose sentiment momentum decelerates, short firms whose sentiment momentum accelerates.
limitations: Single-author repo (PhD student side project), not peer reviewed; author's own H2-2021 hyperparameter validation gate FAILED (IR=-1.50) and was self-overridden rather than passed; OOS alpha t-stat (+1.345) is below the 1.96 significance threshold; WRDS CRSP inputs are subscription-gated and not reproducible by us (we substitute our own PIT universe and SIP bars); repo cites the negation rule as the 'Engelberg-McLean-Pontiff (2018) mean-reversion convention' but the actual EMP2018 paper (see engelberg_mclean_pontiff_2018_abstract_and_finding below) does not state a sentiment-acceleration-reversal rule -- it finds anomaly returns are larger on news days, not that sentiment acceleration reverses; this is the repo author's own extrapolation, not a claim in the cited paper, and the mismatch is now recorded rather than repeated as if EMP2018 said it directly.
independent_replication: No independent third-party replication of this exact repo found; the audit table in section 6 of the README (66/66 pytest cases, look-ahead/purge/PIT-universe/cost-realism checks) is the author's own self-audit, not third-party verification.
impact_on_spec: Fixes the sent_accel feature construction, its sign convention, its data provenance and its deferred (not-yet-built) validation harness before any IC number is computed in this pilot.

claim: Using a sample of 97 stock return anomalies, Engelberg, McLean and Pontiff (2018) find that anomaly returns are 50% higher on corporate news days and six times higher on earnings announcement days; results are most consistent with anomaly returns reflecting biased expectations that are at least partially corrected upon news arrival, rather than dynamic risk or pure data mining.
quote:
Using a sample of 97 stock return anomalies, we find that anomaly returns are 50%
higher on corporate news days and are 6 times higher on earnings announcement
days.
limitations: Working-paper PDF (2017-07-27), not the final published Journal of Finance 2018 typeset version; page/volume citation (73(5), 1971-2001) taken from the repo's own reference list and Wiley's public listing, not independently re-verified against a paywalled publisher copy this pass.
independent_replication: This is itself the original paper; not a replication. Its own within-paper tests (dynamic risk vs mispricing vs data-mining) are the authors' robustness checks, not a third-party replication.
impact_on_spec: Fixes the sent_accel feature construction, its sign convention, its data provenance and its deferred (not-yet-built) validation harness before any IC number is computed in this pilot.

claim: High media pessimism predicts downward pressure on stock market prices followed by a reversion to fundamentals, and unusually high or low pessimism predicts high trading volume; evidence is consistent with noise/liquidity trading rather than media content as a proxy for new fundamental information.
quote:
I find
that high media pessimism predicts downward pressure on market prices followed
by a reversion to fundamentals, and unusually high or low pessimism predicts high
market trading volume.
limitations: Sample is WSJ column-level aggregate market sentiment (not firm-level, not LLM-extracted, not 8-K/news-specific); this is a market-wide timing result, not a cross-sectional stock-picking result, so it supports the sign/mechanism plausibility only, not the specific cross-sectional construction.
independent_replication: Original paper; widely cited (this pass did not re-run an independent replication), used here only as supporting mechanism evidence, not as the tested construction itself.
impact_on_spec: Fixes the sent_accel feature construction, its sign convention, its data provenance and its deferred (not-yet-built) validation harness before any IC number is computed in this pilot.

claim: Presents explicit formulas (also usable as computer code) for 101 real-life quantitative trading alphas built from cross-sectional rank, time-series, and decay operators; average holding period 0.6-6.4 days; average pairwise alpha correlation 15.9%; returns are correlated with volatility but show no significant dependence on turnover.
quote:
We present explicit formulas – that are also computer code – for
101 real-life quantitative trading alphas. Their average holding
period approximately ranges 0.6-6.4 days. The average pair-wise
correlation of these alphas is low, 15.9%.
limitations: The 101 alphas themselves are WorldQuant proprietary trading signals disclosed for research purposes; this paper does not itself contain any LLM, news, or 8-K text signal -- it is cited only for the rank-weighting/operator convention, not as evidence for the sentiment-acceleration mechanism.
independent_replication: Widely reused operator library in the public quant-finance literature and open-source alpha zoos (e.g. Alpha101 implementations); not independently re-verified line-by-line this pass.
impact_on_spec: Fixes the sent_accel feature construction, its sign convention, its data provenance and its deferred (not-yet-built) validation harness before any IC number is computed in this pilot.

claim: Purging and embargoing (Lopez de Prado's terminology) both involve removing some of the data points near the boundaries of affected cross-validation folds in financial time series, to prevent training data whose label window overlaps a test-set label from leaking information across the train/test boundary.
quote: what De Prado calls purging and embargoing . In technical terms, this involves removing some of the data points near the boundaries of affected folds, but there's a subtle difference between the two processes.
limitations: Third-party (QuantInsti) blog explainer of Lopez de Prado's purged/embargoed k-fold CV, not the primary book text (Advances in Financial Machine Learning, 2018, is not freely accessible and is not quoted or redistributed here) -- used only as a plain-language definition to document the deferred, heavier validation step this pilot does not build, not as the authoritative source for a specific numeric parameter.
independent_replication: QuantInsti is a third-party educational provider, independent of De Prado; the underlying method itself has multiple independent open-source implementations (e.g. mlfinlab) not individually re-verified this pass.
impact_on_spec: Fixes the sent_accel feature construction, its sign convention, its data provenance and its deferred (not-yet-built) validation harness before any IC number is computed in this pilot.
